title: Cerebellar Loss Functions

html:
In computational terms, the cerebellum is the optimizer whose objective is closest to supervised predictive calibration. At the level of a local microzone, the cerebellar circuit does not primarily infer a rich latent state, as cortex does, nor does it primarily estimate the long-horizon value of actions, as the basal ganglia do. Instead, it learns a mapping from high-dimensional contextual input to a sparse, module-specific teaching signal: a future motor error, sensory prediction error, timing error, reward-related outcome signal, or cognitive prediction failure. In the idealized language of machine learning, the local cerebellar loss can therefore be written as a regression-like discrepancy between what the microcircuit predicts or cancels and what the climbing-fiber-linked teaching system actually reports 1, 2, 3, 4.

This makes the cerebellar loss both simple and plural. It is simple because the same canonical computation recurs across modules: mossy-fiber inputs are expanded through the granule-cell/parallel-fiber basis, Purkinje cells learn a timed readout, and climbing fibers provide a powerful supervisory signal when prediction and outcome diverge. But it is plural because the content of the target depends on the loop in which the module is embedded. In a vestibulo-ocular module, the target may be retinal slip; in limb control, a kinematic or dynamic error; in eyeblink conditioning, the unexpected presence or omission of an unconditioned stimulus; in reward-linked loops, reward magnitude, omission, or outcome surprise; and in cerebro-cerebellar loops, some still-unresolved form of cognitive or cortical prediction failure 5, 6, 7, 8. This recent study illustrates fig 1 The cerebellar circuitry (Figure). This recent study illustrates fig 2 Cerebellar functional areas and loops (Figure).

This loss is time-structured. The cerebellum is not merely comparing prediction and target at the same instant. Its distinctive function is to learn predictors that lead their teaching signals by tens to hundreds of milliseconds, or, in some behavioral contexts, by longer task-relevant intervals. A cerebellar module is therefore trained to answer: given the current state, context, and efference copy, what error or outcome signal is likely to arrive next, and what correction should already be in place before delayed feedback returns? This is why the cerebellum is naturally framed as a predictive calibrator: its losses are local discrepancies between expected and actual consequences, but those discrepancies are organized around the temporal demands of control 9, 10, 8.

Thus, “the cerebellar loss function” is not one universal biological scalar. It is a family of supervised, module-specific prediction losses: desired versus actual movement state, expected versus actual sensory consequence, predicted versus actual timing, expected versus actual reward or outcome, and perhaps anticipated versus actual cortical or cognitive state. What unifies these cases is not the target’s semantic content, but the learning format: high-dimensional context is used to predict a sparse future teaching event, and the residual error trains the circuit to make the next action, perception, thought, or affective transition unfold with better timing, gain, and continuity 6, 7, 10, 8. Recent human fMRI evidence extends cerebellar prediction-error learning to passive, nonmotor statistical learning (Figure) 48. Recent human fMRI evidence extends cerebellar prediction-error learning to passive, nonmotor statistical learning (Figure).

The proximal local loss: predict or eliminate the future teaching signal

At the most proximal level, the cerebellar loss is the residual predictability of a future teaching signal from the present parallel-fiber context. The Marr-Albus-Ito tradition already cast the cerebellar cortex as a supervised learning device: mossy fibers are expanded through granule cells and parallel fibers, Purkinje-cell output is modified by learned parallel-fiber weights, and climbing fibers provide the sparse instructive signal that tells the circuit when its current output failed to anticipate the relevant event 1, 2, 11, 12, 13. Modern reviews still treat this as the core local algorithm, while emphasizing that Marr, Albus, and Ito differed on the exact meaning of the climbing-fiber signal, the sign of plasticity, and the relation between pattern recognition, control, and internal models 13.

In adaptive-filter language, each Purkinje cell learns a filter from a high-dimensional basis of parallel-fiber signals to an output that removes the predictable component of a later climbing-fiber-linked error. The objective is therefore not literally to silence the inferior olive, but to decorrelate the residual teaching signal from the basis functions that could have predicted it: 𝔼[pi(t−τ)e(t)]→0,\mathbb{E}[p_i(t−\tau)e(t)]\to0, where pi(t−τ)p_i(t−\tau) is a parallel-fiber feature active at the relevant lead time and e(t)e(t) is the later residual teaching signal. At the optimum, parallel-fiber variations should no longer predict climbing-fiber variations, because all predictable structure has already been absorbed into Purkinje/nuclear output 14, 15, 3, 16.

A useful modern restatement is: Purkinje cells learn timed predictions of their climbing-fiber input. Diedrichsen formulates the circuit this way explicitly: high-dimensional parallel-fiber patterns train Purkinje cells to predict climbing-fiber events, often tens to hundreds of milliseconds before the event arrives; in eyeblink conditioning, for example, the granule-cell layer supplies temporal basis functions that allow Purkinje cells to predict the precise time of the unconditioned stimulus 8. This phrasing is slightly different from the older adaptive-filter phrasing. “Decorrelation” describes the optimality condition on the residual signal; “prediction” describes the internal model learned by the circuit. They are two views of the same local loss: once the future teaching event is predicted, it is no longer surprising in the same way, and the residual climbing-fiber signal should be reduced, retimed, or stripped of predictable structure. Granule and climbing-fiber signals can be imaged together (Figure). Granule and climbing-fiber activity track reward timing (Figure). Cerebellar input activity changes with learned reward timing (Figure).

This also prevents an overly narrow interpretation of the loss. In motor loops, the future teaching signal may be retinal slip, limb-state error, dynamic interaction error, or an aversive unconditioned stimulus. In associative learning, recent causal work supports climbing fibers and complex spikes as essential instructive signals for eyeblink conditioning 17. In reward-linked and cognitive loops, however, climbing fibers can carry task-specific variables such as reward prediction, unexpected reward, reward omission, or other outcome-related signals, so the “error” need not be a simple signed motor error 18, 6, 19, 8.

Thus the proximal cerebellar loss can be summarized as: use the present context to predict the future teaching event well enough that the same event no longer arrives as an unmodeled residual. The cerebellum does not need to know, in global semantic terms, whether the signal means “wrong reach,” “mistimed blink,” “unexpected reward omission,” or “failed cortical transition.” That interpretation is supplied by the microzone’s inputs and outputs. Locally, the rule is simpler: learn a precisely timed readout from parallel-fiber context that reduces the future teaching signal’s predictable component, thereby converting delayed errors into anticipatory calibration.

The forward model loss: minimize sensory prediction error

The canonical sensory prediction error loss is the cerebellum’s most familiar special case of predictive calibration. A forward model learns the mapping from current state, context, and efference copy to the sensory consequences that should follow from an action. In motor-control terms, the loss is the discrepancy between the sensory feedback that the system predicts and the sensory feedback that actually arrives:

ℒSPE=∥st+Δt−ŝt+Δt(xt,ut,ct)∥Σ−12,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SPE}} = \left\| s_{t+\Delta t} - \hat{s}_{t+\Delta t}(x_t,u_t,c_t) \right\|^2_{\Sigma^{-1}}, where xtx_t is the estimated current state, utu_t is an efference-copy or motor-command signal, ctc_t is the relevant context, and st+Δts_{t+\Delta t} is delayed sensory feedback. The precision term Σ−1\Sigma^{-1} emphasizes that the loss is not a raw Euclidean mismatch in one sensory channel, but a reliability-weighted prediction error across visual, proprioceptive, vestibular, tactile, and auditory consequences 20, 21, 9.

The need for this loss follows from a basic control problem: sensory feedback arrives too late to stabilize fast movement by itself. A reaching arm, moving eye, vocal tract, or postural controller must act on an estimate of what the body is about to do, not merely on what the sensors reported tens or hundreds of milliseconds ago. A forward model solves this by using efference copy to predict the next sensory state before feedback returns. When the prediction is wrong, the resulting sensory prediction error trains the system to anticipate that consequence more accurately next time 20, 21, 22.

This makes sensory prediction error different from task error. A task error says that the action failed relative to an external goal: the hand missed the target, the cursor landed off-center, or the eye failed to stabilize the image. A sensory prediction error says that the sensory consequence of the motor command was not what the nervous system expected. In visuomotor adaptation, this distinction is crucial: explicit strategies can reduce task error while implicit recalibration continues to be driven by mismatches between predicted and observed feedback. The cerebellar forward-model loss is therefore closer to "my action produced an unexpected sensory consequence" than to "my goal was not achieved" 23, 24, 25.

The vestibulo-ocular reflex provides the cleanest canonical example. The control objective is to keep the retinal image stable while the head moves. If the head turns and the eyes fail to compensate with the correct gain and timing, visual motion remains on the retina as retinal slip. That slip functions as a sensory prediction error for the oculomotor system: the predicted sensory consequence was retinal stability, but the actual consequence was image motion. Cerebellar floccular circuits use vestibular and visual information to calibrate the gain of the reflex, so that future head movements produce anticipatory eye movements that better cancel self-generated retinal motion 26, 27, 28.

Reaching adaptation supplies the analogous limb-control case. When a visuomotor rotation or force field perturbs the normal relation between motor command and sensory consequence, the hand or cursor appears somewhere other than expected. Cerebellum-dependent adaptation uses that mismatch to update the internal model of the limb and environment; patients with cerebellar degeneration are especially impaired at this implicit recalibration, even when they can sometimes use explicit strategies to aim around the perturbation. This supports the view that the cerebellum is not simply choosing better actions, but updating a forward model that predicts the sensory consequences of actions 23, 29, 30.

The same loss also explains sensory cancellation. If the cerebellum predicts the tactile, auditory, or proprioceptive consequences of one’s own action, then predictable reafference can be attenuated while unexpected input remains salient. This is why self-generated touch feels less intense than externally generated touch, and why self-initiated sounds evoke reduced auditory responses. In these cases the forward model does not merely help control the limb; it helps partition the sensory stream into expected consequences of one’s own action and unexpected events from the outside world 31, 32, 33.

At the circuit level, this loss is implemented through the same architecture described above. Mossy fibers carry state, context, sensory, and efference-copy-related information; granule cells expand those signals into a high-dimensional temporal basis; Purkinje cells learn a timed prediction over that basis; and climbing fibers provide sparse teaching events when the predicted and actual sensory consequences diverge. Purkinje-cell simple spikes encode both predictive and feedback-related variables, consistent with the idea that the cerebellar cortex participates in computing the difference between expected and observed consequences 9, 34, 35.

The forward-model loss should therefore be treated as the canonical motor-domain cerebellar objective, but not as the only possible cerebellar objective. It is canonical because it explains the cerebellum’s classic roles in rapid movement, VOR adaptation, reaching adaptation, dysmetria, sensory cancellation, and the compensation of feedback delays. But it is still one member of the broader family of cerebellar losses. In other loops, the future teaching signal may concern reward, timing, autonomic consequence, affective state, or cortical dynamics rather than low-level sensory feedback. The general rule is preserved: use high-dimensional context and efference copy to predict a future consequence, then use the residual mismatch to make the next transition smoother, earlier, and more precise 6, 7, 8.

Temporal granularity and precision as a cerebellar signature

Perhaps the most distinctive cerebellar property is not what is predicted but the temporal regime in which prediction is computed. Cerebellar contributions are repeatedly localized to the subsecond-to-low-second window, with peak sensitivity in the range that spans rapid sensorimotor prediction, conditioned-response timing, and short-interval discrimination 36, 37, 38, 39. Patients with cerebellar damage show increased variability on tasks that require discrete millisecond-scale event timing, perception of short durations, and precisely timed motor responses, while sparing tasks whose timing emerges continuously from movement dynamics 40, 41, 42. Transient cerebellar disruption with rTMS selectively impairs subsecond, not suprasecond, interval estimation 43. The pattern suggests that the cerebellum is not a general-purpose clock but a specialized substrate for predictions whose target lead time is short, sparse, and event-anchored.

The behavioral hallmark of this regime is anticipatory rather than reactive. In delay eyeblink conditioning, the conditioned response is acquired not as a generic blink but as a movement whose amplitude profile peaks just before the unconditioned stimulus, and accurate timing of this anticipation is the primary thing that cerebellar damage degrades 8, 44. Reaching, vestibulo-ocular control, and speech show analogous miscalibration after cerebellar lesions: feedforward correction within a movement is selectively impaired while the slower, feedback-driven scaffolding of the same behaviors is relatively preserved 45, 30. Sensory cancellation has the same temporal flavor: the cerebellum predicts the consequences of self-motion accurately enough that they can be subtracted before they dominate perception, which requires the prediction to lead the reafferent signal by exactly the delay-compensation window in which cerebellar circuits operate 33, 9. In each case the cerebellum is doing the same kind of work: closing a short, structured gap between a present cue and an upcoming consequence. Climbing-fiber stimulation can substitute for the air puff during mouse eyeblink conditioning (Figure). Inhibiting the inferior olive disrupts eyeblink learning (Figure). A mouse study tests direct Purkinje-cell stimulation as a teaching signal (Figure).

This grain constrains what the cerebellum can usefully optimize. A predictor whose teaching signal lands tens to hundreds of milliseconds in the future is well matched to the structured, short-latency mismatches generated by movement, sensory cancellation, conditioned associations, and short-interval estimates. It is less obviously matched to outcomes that arrive seconds or minutes later, where basal-ganglia and prefrontal reinforcement-learning systems appear to carry the relevant credit-assignment work 39, 46. Recent work extends cerebellar contributions to longer intervals via cerebro-cerebellar loops with association cortex, but the underlying computational primitive is unchanged: convert present context into a precisely timed prediction of a future event 36, 47, 10. Temporal precision is therefore best treated as a signature of the cerebellar loss family rather than a loss in itself: whatever the modality of the teaching signal – retinal slip, limb endpoint error, blink-eliciting stimulus, reward outcome, cortical state transition – the cerebellum preferentially absorbs its predictable structure on the side of the timeline that its circuits are configured to resolve. The architectural and plasticity-rule reasons for that configuration belong in "Cerebellar Error Signals" and "Cerebellar Plasticity" 8, 9, 10.

Synthesis

Overall, cerebellar losses are locally supervised prediction losses whose learned models support state estimation and anticipatory control: the same predictive calibration that lets a forward model estimate the current state before feedback returns is what lets the system act early rather than react late.
